passage:
Their hostel room, Tuesday night.
"Damini, you're studying? Your Mamaji's funeral was only yesterday."
"Exam's on Thursday, Siami. Organic chemistry."
"Do you want to talk about him?"
"Not now." Damini underlined a reaction. "I've put him in a box. Just till the exam's over."
"A box?"
"In my head. With a lid. Friday evening I open it."
"Is that... okay?"
"I think so. He'd be furious if I failed because of him. He paid my first-year fees."
Friday evening, same room.
"How was the exam?"
"Good. Really good, actually." Damini's voice wobbled. "Siami, can you sit with me? I'm opening the box now."
Lalremsiami closed her laptop and sat on the bed beside Damini, who cried for a long time, holding her Mamaji's last letter.

qa.q: Which exam did Damini have on Thursday?
qa.a: Organic chemistry.

qa.q: Why did putting her Mamaji 'in a box' feel right to Damini?
qa.a: It let her focus on the exam he would have wanted her to pass, knowing she had set a time to grieve afterwards.

qa.q: What choice made the box helpful rather than harmful?
qa.a: Setting a clear time to open it, Friday evening after the exam, and asking Siami to sit with her while she grieved.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have felt watching Damini study the day after the funeral?
qa.a: Worried and unsure whether it was okay, which is why she asked; she was ready to support Damini when the box opened.

grounding: A student whose uncle has died sets her grief aside to sit an exam, then opens it with her roommate once the exam is over.

passage:
My Dadi died three days before my semester finals. I was nineteen. I remember the phone call, then deciding very calmly: not now. I'll feel this after the last paper. I studied twelve hours a day. I didn't cry at the prayer meeting; I sat at the back with my notes. My cousin Ritu thought I was cold. I wasn't. I had just packed everything into a trunk and sat on the lid.
I topped two papers. Then, on the evening after the last exam, I went to Dadi's room at home, opened her steel cupboard and smelled her talcum powder, and the trunk burst open. I cried for two days. Ritu brought me tea and her old photo album.
Looking back, I, Kalyani, think the trunk helped me get through. But it only worked because I actually opened it.

qa.q: When did Kalyani's Dadi die?
qa.a: Three days before the semester finals.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani decide so calmly, 'not now'?
qa.a: Kalyani wanted to get through the finals and felt grief would swamp the studying, so packing it away felt like the only way to cope for the moment.

qa.q: What made the 'trunk' a healthy pause and not an escape?
qa.a: Opening it after the last exam, going to Dadi's room and letting the grief come, with Ritu there with tea and photos.

qa.q: Why might Ritu have thought Kalyani was cold at the prayer meeting?
qa.a: Ritu saw no tears, only notes, and couldn't see that Kalyani had packed the grief away to open later.

grounding: A student whose grandmother died just before finals boxes up the grief to study, does well, and then lets it out after the last paper.

passage:
Warden's note, Girls' Hostel, 28 April
Vasudha's grandfather died on the 20th, during exam week. She went home for one day for the rites and came back the next evening. Since then she has studied late in the common room, eaten her meals and sat every paper. Her roommate says she hasn't talked about him at all.
She told me, "I'll grieve properly after the 30th. I can't fall apart now." I respect that; setting grief aside for a short while can be a way to cope. But I don't want the box to stay shut for good.
Next step: I've spoken to her. We agreed she'll go home for three days after the last paper, and I've given her the counsellor's number in case the feelings come sooner. I'll check in with her on 1 May.
Parul Sharma, Warden

qa.q: When did Vasudha's grandfather die?
qa.a: On the 20th, during exam week.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha say she couldn't 'fall apart now'?
qa.a: She felt the exams needed all her strength and feared the grief would overwhelm her, so she set it aside for a short time.

qa.q: Which step in Parul's plan makes the pause healthy?
qa.a: Agreeing on three days at home after the last paper and giving the counsellor's number, so there is a set time and support to open the box.

qa.q: What might Vasudha's roommate notice about her during these days?
qa.a: That she studies late and never mentions her grandfather, which may seem strangely calm or quietly worrying.

grounding: A hostel warden notes a student who has set aside grief for her grandfather to get through exams, and makes sure there is a later time to open it.

passage:
Wednesday, 1 am
Minakshi Masi died on Monday. Exams start tomorrow. Mummy said on the phone, "Stay, write your papers. Masi would scold you if you came." So I stayed.
I've done something strange. I've put it all in a box in my head. When I think of her laugh, I say, not now, and go back to thermodynamics. It works. I studied nine hours today. Priya thinks I'm being very brave. I don't know if it's brave. It's just a lid.
But I've promised myself the box gets opened. On the 18th, after the last paper, I'm taking the night bus home. I'll sit in Masi's room with her sewing tin and her old radio and cry as much as I need. I've told Mummy. She said she'll be there.
Until then: lid on. Revise chapter 4.
Sharmila

qa.a: On the 18th, after the last paper, by the night bus.

qa.a: With exams starting, Sharmila is afraid the grief would be overwhelming, so the lid lets Sharmila keep studying instead of stopping at every thought of Masi's laugh.

qa.q: What makes Sharmila's pause healthy rather than just avoidance?

passage: Wasim, you asked how I got through end-sems last year. Okay, here's Rashmi's version. My grandmother died on the second day of exams. Nani, who basically raised me. My mother called at seven in the morning and I had a paper at ten. I remember thinking, very clearly: I'm going to put this in a box. Not now. And I did. I went to the exam. I studied every night. I didn't cry once. I got my best marks ever. But here's the thing I want you to hear. The day after the last paper, I took the train home, sat in Nani's room, and opened the box. I cried for two days straight. My mother held me. If I'd never opened it, I think I'd still be carrying it. The box helped. The opening mattered more.

qa.q: What made Rashmi's way of coping healthy in the end?
qa.a: Rashmi opened the box after the last paper, going home to grieve with the family instead of keeping it shut.

qa.a: She likely felt sad and tender, grieving her own mother and comforting her child at the same time.

passage:
Monday: Jatin's uncle, his mother's brother, died suddenly. Jatin's first end-semester exam was on Wednesday. He called home, then shut his laptop and opened his notes. "Later," he told himself. "I'll feel it later."
Exam week: Jatin studied every night, ate in the mess, and answered every paper. His roommate asked if he was okay. "Fine. After exams." He didn't cry once. He did well.
The Saturday after: Jatin took the bus home to Aligarh. His cousin Lalit, the uncle's son, met him at the gate. They didn't say anything. They sat on the steps where the uncle used to read the paper. Then Jatin started crying, and couldn't stop. Lalit cried too. They stayed there till evening. It was the first time Jatin had let himself feel it, and it felt like breathing out after holding it for a week.

qa.q: When was Jatin's first exam?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: Why did Jatin tell himself "I'll feel it later"?
qa.a: He felt the grief was too big to face with exams two days away, so putting the sorrow aside let him study.

qa.q: What made Jatin's pause healthy rather than harmful?
qa.a: He actually made time after exams to go home and grieve with his cousin, opening the box he'd shut.

qa.q: How might his cousin Lalit have felt when Jatin came home?
qa.a: Lalit probably felt deep sadness and some comfort at having someone to grieve with on his father's steps.

grounding: Shows a student boxing up grief to get through exams and then making time afterwards to grieve with family.

passage: Swati, you're worried because you haven't cried about your grandfather yet, with your exams on? Let me, Urmila Masi, tell you about my final year. My father died in March, a week before my final exams in Nagpur. My mother said, "Your father wanted you to finish." So I made a decision. I put him in a little box inside me. I wrote the exams. I didn't cry, not once. People thought I was hard-hearted. I did very well. But the most important choice I made wasn't the box. It was what I did after. The day after my last paper, I went to the river where he used to take me, alone, and I opened the box. I cried till sunset. And then I kept opening it, bit by bit, over the next year. That's what saved me. Not the closing. The opening.

qa.q: When did Urmila's father die?
qa.a: In March, a week before the final exams.

qa.q: Why did young Urmila decide to put the grief in a box?
qa.a: She felt her father would want her to finish, and setting the sadness aside let her get through the exams.

qa.q: What was the most important choice in the story, and why?
qa.a: Going to the river after the last paper to open the box and grieve, and continuing to do so over the next year, which let her heal.

qa.q: How might the people who thought her hard-hearted have been wrong?
qa.a: They saw only the closed box and didn't know Urmila was holding deep grief until there was time to feel it.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a student setting grief aside during exams and then opening it afterwards to grieve.

Chetan's Nani died on Sunday night. His final exams began on Tuesday morning, the hostel generator had broken, and his train ticket home was for the day after the last paper, because Mummy had insisted: "Nani would want you to finish."

So he put it away. He studied by torchlight with Wasim. He wrote three papers in four days with a steady hand. When Wasim asked, "You okay?" he said, "Later. After the thermodynamics paper."

He did well; he could feel it. Wasim noticed he never once mentioned Nani, not even when his phone lit up with family photos.

The night after the last exam, on the train, Chetan finally opened the photo of Nani at his tenth birthday. He cried from Itarsi to Bhopal. Wasim, travelling with him, just passed tissues and said nothing.

qa.q: Why did Chetan keep saying "Later" when Wasim asked?
qa.a: Chetan was grieving but chose to put the sorrow aside to get through the exams, knowing he couldn't feel it fully and still write.

qa.q: What made Chetan's pause healthy rather than harmful?

qa.q: How might Wasim feel sitting beside Chetan on the train?

passage:
When Shankar's Periappa died, it was the week of his semester exams at the Chennai college. He went to the funeral on Sunday, came back on the night bus, and on Monday morning he was in the exam hall, pen ready.

His roommate Deepak watched him study that week with a strange calm. Shankar made a timetable, stuck to it, ate on time, even ironed his shirt. Once Deepak saw him pick up the steel tiffin box Periappa had given him, pause, and put it away in the cupboard. "After the exams," Shankar said to nobody in particular.

He topped two papers. On the Saturday after the last one, he asked Deepak to come with him to the beach at Besant Nagar, where Periappa used to take him for sundal. They sat there till dark. Shankar talked about Periappa for two hours, and cried, and laughed.

qa.q: Where did Periappa use to take Shankar?
qa.a: Periappa used to take him to the beach at Besant Nagar for sundal.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling when he put the tiffin box away?
qa.a: Shankar was grieving, and putting the box away was a way to set the sadness aside until after the exams.

qa.q: Why was the beach visit an important part of this?
qa.a: It was the later time to open the box; without it, the pause might have hardened into a wall.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt watching Shankar's calm during exam week?
qa.a: Deepak probably felt puzzled and a little worried by the strange calm, and relieved when they finally sat at the beach.

grounding: Shows a student who boxes up grief for his uncle during exams and then opens it at the beach once they are over.

"You've been at that desk since six," Zubin said, leaning on the door frame.
"Organic chemistry is on Thursday."
"Minakshi, Dadu's funeral was yesterday."
"I know." She didn't look up. "If I think about him now, I won't be able to stop. So I'm not thinking about him till Thursday afternoon."
"Is that... okay?"
"I don't know. It's what I can do." She turned a page. "On Thursday, after the paper, I'm going to read his letters. All of them. Will you sit with me?"
Zubin was quiet. "Yeah. I'll bring the tea he liked. Too much cardamom."
She laughed, a little shakily. "Too much cardamom."
On Thursday afternoon they sat on the floor of Dadu's room with the letters and the tea. Minakshi read the first one aloud and didn't get past the second line.

passage:
I was halfway through revising thermodynamics when Irfan came to my hostel room with his phone. It was my father calling to say Dadaji had died that morning. My first exam was in two days. I went home for the cremation, came back the next night, and did something I didn't know I could do. I folded the grief up like a letter and put it in a drawer in my head. I told myself: Dadaji would want me to write the paper. I didn't cry. I studied twelve hours a day. I scored my best marks of the year.
The strange part came after. On the last evening, Irfan and I sat on the hostel roof. He asked, "How are you, really?" and the drawer opened on its own. I cried for an hour. I think the box was a good idea, but only because the roof and Irfan were waiting on the other side.
— Zubin

qa.q: When was Zubin's first exam after Dadaji died?
qa.a: The first exam was in two days.

qa.q: Why did putting the grief away feel right to Zubin during the exams?
qa.a: Zubin believed Dadaji would want the paper written, so shutting the sorrow away felt steadier and safer than falling apart before the exams.

qa.q: What made Zubin's way of coping helpful rather than harmful?
qa.a: There was a later time and a safe person, the evening on the roof with Irfan, when the grief could finally come out.

qa.q: What was it like for Irfan when he asked "How are you, really?"
qa.a: Irfan probably felt worried and caring, and had to stay steady while Zubin cried for an hour.

grounding: A student sets aside grief for a grandfather during exams and later lets it out with a friend, showing the pause helped because it had an end.

passage:
Mentor's note, second year hostel, by Chandrika (faculty mentor)
Madhav's aunt, who raised him for some years, died on 2 March. Semester exams began on 6 March. Madhav returned after three days at home and told me, "I'll deal with it after exams." Since then he has attended every class, eaten in the mess, and studied in the library until closing. His friends say he doesn't mention his aunt at all. His first two papers went well.
I have not pushed him to talk. Setting it aside seems to be working for now, and he knows my door is open. What worries me is if the exams end and there is no space to grieve.
What I did next: I told Madhav I would meet him on 20 March, the day after the last exam, just to see how he is. I also booked a slot with the campus counsellor for that week, and he agreed to go.

qa.q: When did the semester exams begin?
qa.a: Semester exams began on 6 March.

qa.q: Why might Madhav's "I'll deal with it after exams" feel reasonable to him?
qa.a: He probably feels deep sadness but also fear of falling apart before exams, so putting the grief aside feels like a safe way to get through them.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do to make sure the grief had a time to come out?
qa.a: Chandrika set a meeting for the day after the last exam and booked a slot with the campus counsellor that week.

qa.q: How might Madhav's friends see his silence about his aunt?
qa.a: His friends might feel unsure and worried, not knowing whether to mention her or leave him alone.

grounding: A mentor's note shows a student boxing up grief for an aunt during exams and the mentor planning a time for the box to open afterwards.

passage:
Monday night, hostel
Exam three done. Circuits. I think it went well, which feels odd to write when Nani died eight days ago.
I've been doing a thing where I put her in a box. Not forget her, just close the lid while I study. Tonight I almost broke it. Tanvir was eating the laddoos his mother sent, and they smelt exactly like the ones Nani made. My throat went tight. I left the room, walked round the block twice, came back and opened my notes. Lid shut again.
But I'm scared of what happens if I never open it. So I made a plan with Tanvir. Friday is the last paper. Saturday morning we take the bus to Nani's house. I'll sit in her kitchen and let it all out. Tanvir says he'll come and just sit there with me.
Two more papers. Lid stays shut till Saturday.
Dhruv

qa.q: What did the laddoos Tanvir was eating smell like?
qa.a: They smelt exactly like the ones Nani made.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when the laddoos' smell hit, and how did Dhruv cope?
qa.a: Dhruv felt a sudden wave of grief, with a tight throat, and coped by walking round the block twice before studying again.

qa.q: Why is Dhruv's Saturday plan a wise one?
qa.a: It gives the grief a set time and place, Nani's kitchen with Tanvir beside, so the box has a door and isn't shut forever.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel about going with Dhruv on Saturday?
qa.a: Tanvir may feel caring and a bit unsure, but willing to just sit there and be company.

grounding: A student writes in a diary about keeping grief for a grandmother shut away for exams and planning a time after exams to let it out.
